nodes.summary: For every positive integer $n$ and every real number $\alpha$, the Beatty term $b_n(\alpha)$ equals the natural-number floor of $n/\alpha$: the largest natural number $m$ with $m \le n/\alpha$ when $n/\alpha \ge 0$, and $0$ when $n/\alpha < 0$. Division by zero is read as $0$, so $n/0 = 0$.
nodes.title: Beatty term as a natural-number floor

nodes.title: Beatty sequences are almost Beatty

nodes.summary: For a positive integer $n$ and a real number $\alpha$, the Beatty term $b_n(\alpha)$ is the natural number $\max(\lfloor n/\alpha \rfloor, 0)$: the $n$-th term $\lfloor n \cdot (1/\alpha) \rfloor$ of the Beatty sequence of slope $1/\alpha$, truncated at $0$. Division by zero is read as $0$, so $b_n(0) = 0$.

nodes.title: Almost Beatty sequence

nodes.summary: Three sequences $s_1, s_2, s_3$ of natural numbers indexed by the positive integers partition the positive integers when their ranges are pairwise disjoint, that is, $s_i(m) \ne s_j(n)$ for all $i \ne j$ and all positive integers $m$ and $n$, and the union of their ranges is exactly the set of positive integers: a natural number $k$ is a value of some $s_i$ if and only if $k > 0$.
